walkthroughs.body_html:
Decision Making to Improve Operational Performance — a core area of A-Level Business Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Decision Making to Improve Operational Performance brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Decision Making to Improve Operational Performance.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A likely benefit of high capacity utilisation is:
options: Fixed costs are spread over more units, cutting unit costs
More spare capacity to take on sudden new orders
Less pressure on machinery and staff
Higher stock-holding costs
Continuous improvement in small steps, involving employees
A one-off radical restructuring of the business
Outsourcing production to overseas suppliers
A method of mass advertising in Japan

mcqs.q: Is 100% capacity utilisation the ideal target for a business?
options: A business should always aim to run at 100% capacity.
Usually not — at full capacity there is no slack for maintenance, breakdowns or sudden orders, and quality and morale can suffer; a high but not full level is often preferred.
Capacity utilisation cannot legally exceed 90%.
Quality assurance is a type of insurance policy bought from banks.

mcqs.q: Does just-in-time stock control always reduce costs?
options: JIT is risk-free because holding no stock can only save money.
It cuts storage and waste costs, but it relies on dependable suppliers, sacrifices bulk-buying discounts, and leaves the firm exposed if deliveries fail.
JIT means stock is delivered just in time for the annual stocktake.
Quality assurance is a type of insurance policy bought from banks.

mcqs.q: Are quality control and quality assurance the same thing?
options: Quality assurance is a type of insurance policy bought from banks.
No — quality control inspects output after production to catch defects, while quality assurance builds prevention into every stage so defects are less likely to occur.
Capacity utilisation cannot legally exceed 90%.
Checking finished products is all a business needs to do to guarantee quality.
